shortQuestions: Vegetable oils contain a high proportion of unsaturated fatty acids with C=C double bonds.

Oxygen of the air attacks these double bonds (oxidative rancidity), forming peroxides that break down into aldehydes and ketones with unpleasant smells and tastes; moisture, light, heat and microbes also hydrolyse the oil into free fatty acids (hydrolytic rancidity).
So oils go rancid faster than saturated fats; antioxidants and airtight storage slow it down.

Saturated fatty acids have straight hydrocarbon chains that pack closely together, giving strong van der Waals forces between molecules — so more energy is needed to melt them (e.g. stearic acid m.p. 70 °C).
Cis double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids put kinks in the chains, so they pack loosely with weaker forces and melt at lower temperatures (oleic acid m.p. 13 °C).

(a) Glucose is an aldohexose (–CHO group; usually a six-membered pyranose ring) and is dextrorotatory; fructose is a ketohexose (C=O at C2; five-membered furanose ring in sucrose) and is laevorotatory.
(b) Sucrose is glucose + fructose joined α1→β2 through both anomeric carbons, so it is non-reducing; maltose is glucose + glucose joined α1→4, so it is a reducing sugar.

(c) Cellulose is a linear polymer of β-glucose (β-1,4 links), a structural polysaccharide that humans cannot digest and that gives no colour with iodine; starch is a polymer of α-glucose (amylose α-1,4 and branched amylopectin α-1,6), a storage food that humans digest and that gives a blue-black colour with iodine.
DNA stores the genetic (hereditary) information of the cell in the sequence of its bases.
DNA replicates and passes the genetic information from parent cells to daughter cells (heredity).

RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) carries out protein synthesis by transcribing and translating the genetic code, thus controlling all cell activities. (Nucleotides such as ATP also act as energy carriers and coenzymes.)
Sucrose is hydrolysed by dilute acid or the enzyme invertase (sucrase):
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose).
The equimolar mixture is called invert sugar because the sign of optical rotation changes from + (sucrose) to − (fructose is strongly laevorotatory).

Denaturation destroys the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of a protein: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide links and hydrophobic interactions are broken by heat, strong acids/bases, heavy-metal ions, alcohol, radiation or shaking.

The primary structure (peptide bonds) remains, but the protein unfolds, loses its biological activity (enzymes stop working), becomes less soluble and often coagulates — e.g. boiled egg white or curdled milk. It is usually irreversible.
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three components:

(1) a pentose sugar — deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA; (2) a phosphate group; (3) a nitrogenous base — purines adenine (A) and guanine (G), pyrimidines cytosine (C) and thymine (T, in DNA) or uracil (U, in RNA).
Nucleotides are joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.
Primary: the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, joined by peptide bonds.
Secondary: regular folding of the chain into an α-helix or β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
Tertiary: the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain, held by interactions between side chains (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bridges, hydrophobic forces).
Quaternary: the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) in one functional protein, e.g. haemoglobin with four chains.

Non-competitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site, on either the free enzyme or the enzyme–substrate complex; it changes the enzyme's shape. Vmax decreases while Km is unchanged; adding substrate does not reverse it.
Uncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, not to the free enzyme. Both Vmax and Km decrease.

Physical properties: lipids are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (ether, chloroform, benzene); they are greasy, less dense than water and poor conductors of heat; fats (mostly saturated) are solid and oils (unsaturated) liquid at room temperature; pure lipids are colourless and odourless.

Chemical properties: hydrolysis by acids or lipase gives glycerol and fatty acids; saponification with NaOH gives soap and glycerol; hydrogenation of oils (Ni catalyst) gives solid fats (vanaspati ghee); addition of iodine/halogens to C=C (iodine number measures unsaturation); oxidation by air causes rancidity.
longQuestions: (a) Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or substances that give these on hydrolysis; most have the formula Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ. Classification by the number of sugar units on hydrolysis: (i) Monosaccharides — cannot be hydrolysed further; classified by number of carbons (trioses, pentoses, hexoses) and functional group (aldoses, e.g. glucose, ribose; ketoses, e.g. fructose). (ii) Oligosaccharides — 2–10 units; disaccharides: sucrose, maltose, lactose. (iii) Polysaccharides — many units; starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin. They are also classed as reducing or non-reducing, and as sugars (sweet, soluble) or non-sugars.

(b) Role in health: glucose is the main fuel of cells (essential for the brain and red blood cells); glycogen stores energy in liver and muscles; dietary fibre (cellulose) aids digestion, prevents constipation and lowers cholesterol; ribose and deoxyribose form nucleic acids; glycoproteins act in cell recognition.

Diseases: diabetes mellitus — lack of insulin or insulin resistance causes high blood glucose; excess sugar intake leads to obesity, tooth decay and heart disease; hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) causes dizziness and fainting; lactose intolerance (lack of lactase) causes bloating and diarrhoea; galactosaemia and glycogen-storage diseases are inherited disorders.

(a) Classification of proteins: (i) By composition — simple proteins give only amino acids on hydrolysis (albumins, globulins, histones, glutelins, scleroproteins such as keratin and collagen); conjugated proteins contain a non-protein prosthetic group (glycoproteins — mucin; lipoproteins; nucleoproteins; chromoproteins — haemoglobin; phosphoproteins — casein; metalloproteins — ferritin); derived proteins are formed by partial hydrolysis or denaturation (proteoses, peptones, peptides).

(ii) By shape — fibrous proteins: long, insoluble, structural (keratin of hair, collagen, myosin, silk fibroin); globular proteins: compact, water-soluble, functional (enzymes, insulin, haemoglobin, antibodies). (iii) By function — enzymes, hormones (insulin), transport (haemoglobin), structural (collagen), contractile (actin, myosin), defensive (antibodies), storage (casein, ovalbumin).

(b) Properties: high molecular masses and colloidal solutions; amphoteric (contain –NH₂ and –COOH), with an isoelectric point at which solubility is lowest; denatured by heat, acids, alkalis, heavy metals and alcohol; hydrolysed by acids, alkalis or enzymes into amino acids; optically active; precipitated by salts and heavy-metal ions; colour tests — biuret (violet), xanthoproteic (yellow with HNO₃), Millon's (red), ninhydrin (purple).

(a) Lipids are naturally occurring esters of fatty acids (and related compounds) that are insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar organic solvents. Classification: (i) Simple lipids — esters of fatty acids with alcohols: fats and oils (triglycerides of glycerol) and waxes (esters of long-chain alcohols). (ii) Compound lipids — esters containing extra groups: phospholipids (lecithin, cephalin), glycolipids, lipoproteins. (iii) Derived lipids — obtained by hydrolysis or related: fatty acids, glycerol, steroids (cholesterol, sex hormones), fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K.

(b) Structure: a fat or oil is a triglyceride — glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, which may be saturated (palmitic C₁₅H₃₁COOH, stearic C₁₇H₃₅COOH) or unsaturated (oleic, linoleic, linolenic). Phospholipids have one fatty acid replaced by a phosphate group, giving a polar head and two non-polar tails.

Nutritional importance: the most concentrated source of energy (about 37 kJ g⁻¹, twice that of carbohydrates); supply essential fatty acids (linoleic, linolenic) that the body cannot make; carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; improve taste and satiety.

Biological importance: energy storage in adipose tissue; thermal insulation and protection of organs; phospholipids and cholesterol form cell membranes; steroids act as hormones (testosterone, oestrogen, cortisol) and cholesterol forms vitamin D and bile salts; prostaglandins regulate body processes. Excess saturated fat and cholesterol contribute to obesity, atherosclerosis and heart disease.

(a) Enzyme inhibitors are substances that reduce the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions. Reversible inhibitors: competitive — structurally similar to the substrate, they bind to the active site and compete with it (e.g. malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase; sulpha drugs block bacterial folate synthesis); raising substrate concentration overcomes them. Non-competitive — bind elsewhere and change the shape of the enzyme (heavy-metal ions at low levels); uncompetitive — bind to the enzyme–substrate complex. Irreversible inhibitors bind covalently and permanently destroy the active site (nerve gases on acetylcholinesterase, cyanide on cytochrome oxidase, aspirin on cyclooxygenase, penicillin on bacterial transpeptidase).

Role: natural inhibitors regulate metabolic pathways (feedback inhibition — the end product inhibits an early enzyme); many drugs, antibiotics and pesticides act as enzyme inhibitors; some poisons kill by inhibiting vital enzymes.
(b) Structural components: both DNA and RNA are polynucleotides; each nucleotide = pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base, linked by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds into a sugar–phosphate backbone.

DNA: sugar deoxyribose; bases A, G, C and T; two antiparallel strands coiled into a double helix, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A=T, G≡C); found mainly in the nucleus. RNA: sugar ribose; bases A, G, C and U (uracil instead of thymine); usually single-stranded; three types — mRNA, tRNA and rRNA; found mainly in the cytoplasm.

(a) Enzymes are protein biocatalysts. They speed up reactions (often millions of times) by providing an active site where the substrate binds (lock-and-key or induced-fit model), forming an enzyme–substrate complex that lowers the activation energy; they are highly specific, work under mild conditions (37 °C, near-neutral pH), are needed only in small amounts and are not used up.

Digestion of food: salivary amylase converts starch to maltose in the mouth; pepsin (stomach, pH ≈ 2) breaks proteins into peptides; in the small intestine pancreatic amylase, trypsin and chymotrypsin, and lipase (with bile) digest starch, proteins and fats; maltase, sucrase and lactase split disaccharides into monosaccharides; peptidases give amino acids. Thus large insoluble molecules are converted into small, soluble, absorbable ones.

(b) Temperature: the rate rises with temperature (more collisions) up to an optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes); above it the enzyme is denatured and activity falls sharply; at low temperature enzymes are inactive but not destroyed.

pH: each enzyme works best at an optimum pH (pepsin ≈ 2, salivary amylase ≈ 6.8, trypsin ≈ 8); other pH values change the ionisation of groups in the active site and can denature the enzyme. Other factors: substrate concentration (rate rises then levels off at Vmax when the enzyme is saturated), enzyme concentration (rate proportional to it), cofactors/activators and inhibitors.

(a) Zinc is an essential trace element: it is a cofactor of more than 300 enzymes (carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase, DNA and RNA polymerases); it is needed for protein synthesis, cell division and growth, wound healing, the immune system, the storage and action of insulin, sperm production, and the senses of taste and smell.

Zinc deficiency causes slow wound healing, stunted growth, loss of appetite and taste, skin problems, hair loss, poor immunity and delayed sexual development. Sources: meat, fish, eggs, nuts, whole grains and pulses.

(b) Calcium: deficiency causes rickets in children (soft, bent bones), osteomalacia and osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) in adults, tetany and muscle cramps, poor blood clotting and weak teeth; excess can cause kidney stones and hypercalcaemia.

Phosphorus: needed with calcium for bones and teeth and for ATP, DNA and phospholipids. Deficiency (rare) leads to weak bones, rickets, muscle weakness and fatigue; excess phosphate (e.g. in kidney failure or very high soft-drink intake) upsets the calcium balance, causing bone loss and calcium deposits in soft tissues. Vitamin D and parathyroid hormone control the Ca/P balance.
activities: On adding lemon juice or vinegar to warm milk, the milk curdles: white solid lumps (curd) separate from a clear yellowish-green liquid (whey).
The milk changes from a uniform liquid (colloid) into a solid mass of curds suspended in a watery liquid — it coagulates.
Yes. The milk protein casein is denatured and precipitated; this is a chemical change and cannot be reversed by simply removing the acid.

Yes. The acid lowers the pH of milk (about 6.7) to the isoelectric point of casein (about pH 4.6). The negative charges on the casein micelles are neutralised, so they no longer repel each other and they clump together (coagulate). Warming speeds this up.
The products are casein (curd, which can be pressed into cottage cheese/paneer) and whey.

Yes. Casein is a high-quality phosphoprotein containing all the essential amino acids, together with calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth. Whey also contains useful proteins, lactose, minerals and B vitamins.

Curd/casein is used to make paneer, cheese and other dairy products; casein is also used in protein supplements and infant foods, and industrially in glues, paints, paper coatings and casein plastics. Whey is used in whey-protein drinks and baked foods.
